chapter_theme: Songs at Kailasa (கயிலைமலை): two yogic pleas for the self to become Siva's form in light, nada and bliss, three confessions of courtesans who take a man's wealth, a life from the womb, and a short prayer for the gift of song that Sambandar had; the praise dwells on Siva's dance, his swallowing of the poison and the demon who lifted Kailasa.
structure_note: 517 and 518 are yogic; 519 and 522 confess courtesans; 520 runs from the womb to a ruined life; 521 is an eight-line song asking for poetry.

517.reading: A yogic plea: the poet asks that, with the breath's two paths closed, he go by the path of Siva to the one beyond, join Siva's light as in a marriage, his two deeds roasted, and enter the golden land beyond darkness and sun, where the body is made steady and both melt into one. The praise is Siva's dance, with anklets deafening the eight directions, the three gods and the Vedas bowing, trident, axe and deer whirling, Adisesha's crowns crackling and devotees crying 'Hara Hara', and Murugan as Uma's son, at Kailasa of the devotees.
517.nuance: காலின் இருவழி அடைபட்டு, the two ways of the breath closed, and சிவசுடர் ... மணமென மருவி, joining Siva's light as in marriage, are the stages of the ascent. The second half of the plea does not split cleanly, and what is asked at its end (இளையவன் என வித்தாரம்) is not clear to me.

518.reading: The poet asks that his bound deeds be powdered, his self become Siva's form, the 'I' and the flesh fall away, and that in the light of nada and Brahman knowledge well up so that he rejoices daily in bliss and attainment; he asks for the feet. The praise names Siva, our father, whose hand took the ocean's poison so that the sky, the poet, Brahma and Vishnu might live, Murugan with the bee-hummed kadamba garland, and Kailasa, where Valli delights.
518.nuance: சீவன் சிவச்சொருபம் என தேறி and நானென்பது அற்று, the self found to be Siva's form and the 'I' gone, are the language of union. The opening likens the hoped-for grace to honey, the three fruits, milk, cane and tender coconut, but its last words are corrupt.

519.reading: The poet speaks of women who laugh, stare, threaten, act and polish their faces to stir infatuation, and gather the wealth that comes, and asks whether he must fall into the net of these thieving women. The praise names Murugan who cut off the demons' heads, rode the dark peacock and embraced the girl of the millet field, the Lord of the white mountain, who keeps a woman in his spread matted hair and holds the deer.
519.nuance: திருட்டு முலைப்பெண் மருட்டு வலை, the deluding net of thieving women, names deceit and theft together. The closing marks, Ganga in the matted hair and the deer in the hand, are Siva's, here given to Murugan.

520.reading: The poet traces his life from a drop like dew in the womb, growing small as a seed and then as large as palm and coconut fruit, slipping head down to earth as a doll of nine gates moved by the rope of breath, crawling and crying at his mother's breast, and then, through past wrongs, forgetting virtue until his mind was ruined and his body stank; he asks now for the anklets. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which the vel is thrown with a smile, and names Siva, Ganapati and Murugan rejoicing at Kailasa, and his union with the kurinji girl.
520.nuance: ஒன்பது வாசல் சேர் உருவம் ... வளிகயிறினுடன் ஆடி, a figure of nine gates dancing on the rope of breath, makes the body a puppet. இனி, now, is the turn from the life told to the plea.

521.reading: A short song: the poet asks to be given, as Murugan's servant, the gift of singing garlands of immortal poems like the wise one of Pugali, lord on earth. The praise names the lone vel thrown against the Asuras and Murugan as the meaning of Namasivaya, Lord of the silver mountain.
521.nuance: புகலியில் வித்தகர் is Sambandar of Sirkazhi (Pugali), the model of the poet-saint; the plea is to be a poet as he was. நமசிவயப் பொருளானே makes Murugan the meaning of Siva's five syllables.

522.reading: The poet speaks of courtesans who polish their faces, loosen their breast-bands, deceive and snatch a man's goods, invite him to bed, laugh, kiss and grip his neck, and asks whether he must perish daily trembling for them. The praise names Murugan as son of the one who dances for the world in drum syllables, who gives attainment to devotees who think of him, and the Lord at Kailasa, which the demon heaved up, who powdered and trampled the other mountain.
522.nuance: பொருட்பறித்து, snatching wealth, marks the courtesan. The end tells of the demon (Ravana, by his deed) who lifted Kailasa; whether மற்ற பொருப்பைப் பொடித்து, powdering the other mountain, means Krauncha is my guess.

links.note: Both begin the life with a drop like dew (பனிபோல், பனியின் விந்துளி) and follow it head down out of the womb to the crawling child; 508 goes on to women and Death, 520 to past deeds and a ruined mind.

Thiruppugazh 517 begins its ascent with காலின் இருவழி அடைபட்டு, the breath's two ways shut, before going by the path of Siva to the one beyond. Tirumanthiram 795 names the harm of the breath that runs இடம் வலம், left and right, without keeping to the middle, and says joy comes when it is led as it should go. Read together, the song's two closed ways are the Tirumanthiram's left and right channels, and both make stopping them the first step.

Thiruppugazh 518 asks that the soul, its deeds powdered, come to know itself as Siva's form (சீவன் சிவச்சொருபம் என தேறி). Tirumanthiram 2017 says there is no difference between சீவன் and சிவன, and that once souls know Siva they remain as Siva. Both make the change a matter of knowing (தேறி, அறிந்தபின்), not of becoming something new.

Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of யான் எனது, I and mine, enters a world higher than the gods'. Thiruppugazh 518 asks for நானென்பது அற்று, the 'I' gone, together with the flesh, and places the goal in the light of nada and Brahman where knowledge wells up as bliss. The song takes the Kural's renunciation of 'I' and names what lies past it in the language of union rather than of a higher world.

Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which worthless men sink (ஆழும்). Thiruppugazh 519 lists the laughter, stares, threats and acting of thieving women who gather a man's wealth, and asks whether he must fall (விழுவேனோ) into their deluding net. Both make the courtesan's embrace a place one falls into; the song gives the arts that set the trap, the Kural the verdict on who sinks.

Kural 1020 likens the movements of the shameless to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) that feigns life by its string (நாணால்). Thiruppugazh 520 makes the newborn body of nine gates a doll (பதுமையின் செயல் போலவே) dancing on a rope of breath (வளிகயிறினுடன் ஆடி). The Kural uses the puppet for a man without inner shame; the song extends it to every embodied life, whose string is the breath itself.

Tirumanthiram 487 says one born of two who met in pleasure and grown within painful bondage (துன்புறு பாசத்தில்) can, once in the world, still seek the Ancient. Thiruppugazh 520 tells the life from the drop in the womb through birth and a ruined youth and then turns with இனி, now, to ask for the feet. Both set the turn to the Lord after a birth and growth told as bondage, and both hold it still possible.

Thiruppugazh 521 asks Murugan for the gift of singing immortal poems like the wise one of Pugali (புகலியில் வித்தகர்), Sambandar. Thiruppugazh 1282 says Murugan himself, as Sambandar (சம்பந்தனென), filled the land with Tamil. Read together, the poet in 521 asks for Sambandar's gift from the one the book elsewhere names as Sambandar.

Naladiyar 377 says the worthless woman licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from a man's hands (நக்கி அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு), and those fooled (ஏமாந்து) into thinking her love theirs are laughed at. Thiruppugazh 522 has the courtesans deceive (எத்தி மழுப்பி), snatch goods (பொருட்பறித்து) and give kisses and embraces, and the poet fears perishing daily for them. Both tie the caress directly to the taking of wealth; the Naladiyar ends in ridicule, the song in daily ruin.

source_issues: Song 518: line 2 is corrupt (பழ஧த்தசிவ ...... ம ளுறத்), with a bad glyph ஧ and a broken word; the sense of the opening image cannot be completed.
